paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: God was working in Ruth's ordinary morning. She asked to glean, which was just a plan to get some food. She walked out and "happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz" (Ruth 2:3). Nobody in that field was announcing a big moment, and the passage never says Ruth knew what was going on, but the passage puts her right where help was waiting.

Look at what Boaz says about her, though. He tells her, "May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge" (Ruth 2:12). Ruth came to a people she did not know before, and Boaz says she found refuge with the God of Israel. Then Boaz becomes part of the answer, with protection, water, a meal with some left over, and stalks left for her to gather (Ruth 2:9, 14, 16).

And Naomi hears all this and says the LORD "has not withdrawn His kindness from the living or the dead" (Ruth 2:20). I think that's the heart of it for you, baker. When your days feel small and your plans feel plain, you can keep showing up and doing the next faithful thing, because God's kindness is already at work in the field you're standing in. I spent years in a junk drawer thinking I was forgotten, and I'm telling you, the LORD was not done. This story isn't over, either.
